title: Explain a protein activity change
context: Original data: at the same temperature and enzyme concentration, initial rates are 18, 44 and 11 units/min at pH 5, 7 and 9 respectively. Each value is a mean from independent replicates; uncertainty estimates have not been supplied.
prompts: Identify the independent variable and the dependent variable, including units.
Describe the observed pattern using at least two numerical values.
Explain a molecular mechanism that could contribute to this pattern.
Name one missing piece of evidence that limits a claim about the differences.
criteria: The manipulated factor is pH; measured initial activity is in units/min.
The mean rate is highest at pH 7 (44), compared with 18 at pH 5 and 11 at pH 9. These data alone do not locate the precise optimum.
pH can change protonation, molecular interactions or active-site chemistry, affecting catalysis. A specific irreversible folding change is not established.
Useful missing evidence includes replicate counts, variability, detector controls, or a matched recovery assay. Mean differences alone do not establish statistical significance.

title: Predict osmosis under stated conditions
context: Original model: a water-permeable membrane separates 0.30 M nonpenetrating solute inside a cell from 0.10 M outside. Both sides are at 300 K with pressure potential initially zero. Use i=1 and R=0.0831 L·bar/(mol·K).
prompts: Calculate initial solute potential on each side.
Predict the initial net direction of water movement and justify it.
Explain how increasing internal pressure could alter the result in a walled cell.
State why a readily penetrating solute would require additional information.
criteria: Inside: −7.479 bar; outside: −2.493 bar. Include the negative sign and pressure assumption.
Water initially moves inward, from the higher external potential to the lower internal potential.
Positive internal pressure raises total internal water potential and can oppose further entry until potentials balance.
Permeating solutes can redistribute, changing the effective osmotic relationship over time; permeability and time scale matter.

title: Test a change in energetic coupling
context: Original experiment: an isolated mitochondrial preparation receives electron donors and oxygen. After compound X is added, measured oxygen consumption continues but ATP production decreases. Untreated preparations are measured in parallel.
prompts: Identify a control and one additional variable to keep constant.
Propose a mechanism consistent with continued electron flow but reduced ATP production.
Explain a measurement that would test that proposed mechanism.
State why the observations do not uniquely identify compound X.
criteria: The untreated preparation is a control; possible constants include mitochondrial amount, temperature, substrate supply and assay duration.
A proton leak or reduced coupling can dissipate the gradient used by ATP synthase while electron flow continues. This is a hypothesis rather than a proven identity.
Measure a membrane-potential or proton-gradient indicator and compare treated with matched untreated preparations.
Other disruptions or assay effects could produce some of the pattern; additional tests are needed to distinguish causes.

title: Locate a signaling dependency
context: Original model: receptor R activates kinase A, which activates kinase B, which is required for response Z. Inhibiting A removes Z. A constitutively active B restores Z even while A is inhibited. Assume there are no other required branches in this model.
prompts: Predict whether ligand binding can remain normal during A inhibition.
Explain what the rescue result supports about pathway order.
Predict the effect of inactivating B while R and A remain active.
Explain why the no-other-branches assumption matters.
criteria: Binding can remain normal because the proposed defect lies downstream of reception.
Active B bypasses the need for A in the stated model, supporting B as a downstream component.
The required response is reduced or absent because active upstream components cannot replace required B activity.
Additional branches could require A for other essential functions, preventing a simple bypass from restoring the response.

title: Interpret an inheritance sample
context: Original cross: two heterozygous parents, Aa × Aa, with complete dominance and equal survival among genotypes. Of 80 offspring, 62 show the dominant phenotype and 18 the recessive phenotype.
prompts: Calculate expected phenotype counts under the stated model.
Calculate χ² = Σ(O−E)²/E.
For two fixed-probability categories, use df=1 and critical value 3.841 at α=0.05 to state a decision.
Explain why that decision does not prove the model.
criteria: Expected counts are 60 dominant and 20 recessive.
0.2667 is below 3.841, so fail to reject the stated model under the test assumptions.
Sampling can produce deviations, the test has limited power, and other models may also fit. Failure to reject is not proof.

title: Distinguish expression from protein function
context: Original comparison: an edited regulatory region leaves a gene’s coding sequence unchanged. Relative mRNA abundance falls from 1.0 to 0.25, while activity per purified protein molecule is unchanged.
prompts: Calculate the percent decrease in relative mRNA abundance.
Explain why protein sequence need not change.
Predict a possible effect on total cellular activity and give a limitation.
Propose a measurement that distinguishes lower abundance from lower activity per molecule.
criteria: A regulatory-region change can alter transcription without changing the coding sequence.
Less mRNA may reduce protein abundance and total activity, but translation, turnover and compensation can alter the outcome.
Measure protein amount separately from total activity, and normalize activity to protein amount under matched conditions.

title: Use a population null model
context: Original model: a diploid population is assumed to meet Hardy–Weinberg conditions at a two-allele locus. Recessive phenotype frequency is 0.16 under complete dominance.
prompts: Infer q and p under the stated assumptions.
Calculate expected heterozygote frequency and count among 250 individuals.
Name one process that can change allele frequencies.
Explain why a deviation from expected counts does not uniquely demonstrate selection.
criteria: q=√0.16=0.4 and p=0.6. These are model-dependent inferences.
2pq=0.48; expected heterozygote count is 120.
Examples include selection, drift, mutation or gene flow, with an explanation linking the process to allele-frequency change.
Sampling, nonrandom mating, migration or other departures can also affect the comparison. A mechanism needs additional evidence.

title: Reason about an ecosystem perturbation
context: Original experiment: in replicated lake enclosures, nutrient addition is followed by higher algal biomass and later lower dissolved oxygen than in matched controls. Temperature and water volume are held similar, but decomposition has not been measured directly.
prompts: Describe the observed associations without assuming a unique mechanism.
Explain a plausible chain linking nutrient input to later oxygen loss.
Propose an additional measurement that tests the proposed chain.
State a limitation of extending enclosure results to an entire lake.
criteria: Treated enclosures have greater algal biomass and subsequently lower oxygen than controls under the reported conditions.
Nutrients may increase production; additional organic matter can support decomposition-associated respiration that consumes oxygen.
Measure microbial respiration, decomposition rate or organic-matter changes over time, alongside oxygen and matched controls.
Whole lakes can differ in mixing, species interactions, transport, scale and environmental variability. The model captures only selected conditions.
